publication.title: September 20 briefing: a Yom Kippur eve terror attack in the West Bank, Gaza strikes on October 7 operatives, and a sharper Iran-US standoff
publication.summary: A gunman killed Netanel Shukrun, 36, at a West Bank spring on the eve of Yom Kippur; the IDF's Duvdevan unit arrested the assailant hours later, and Prime Minister Netanyahu ordered reinforcements and vowed to "hold them all accountable" in Gaza, Lebanon and Judea and Samaria. The IDF said three Hamas operatives, including two identified as October 7 participants, were killed in weekend Gaza strikes. Separately, Iran's military said it had been informed of a US plan to resume strikes and threatened to respond by targeting American allies, and Israel's institutional response to the NAZA documentary escalated further.
publication.body:
## A Yom Kippur eve attack in the West Bank

Netanel Shukrun, 36, a father of six from Alei Zahav, was shot and killed on September 20 at the Ein Raya spring in the central West Bank while visiting the site with his son, according to the Jerusalem Post and Haaretz. Israeli reporting described the gunman firing from a vehicle with Palestinian Authority plates before fleeing on foot; the IDF said Duvdevan counterterrorism soldiers, acting on Shin Bet and Israel Police intelligence, arrested the suspect roughly three hours later at a nearby hospital. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said "no terrorist is immune, nor are those who assisted them," and that Israel "will hold them all accountable — in Gaza, in Lebanon, and in Judea and Samaria," ordering security-force reinforcements to the West Bank along with closures and arrests. Full details are on the dedicated report below.

## Gaza: October 7 operatives among those killed in weekend strikes

The IDF said three Hamas operatives were killed in strikes over the weekend, including two identified as having taken part in the October 7, 2023 attack. Separately, wire reporting described two Palestinians wounded by Israeli gunfire near Khan Yunis in southern Gaza. Exact circumstances of the Khan Yunis incident were not independently confirmed beyond initial wire coverage at the time of writing.

## Iran-US tensions resurface

Iran's military command said on September 20 that it had been informed of US plans to resume strikes on Iran, and stated it would respond by targeting American allies in the region, according to the Times of Israel's live coverage. No further operational detail was available in the sources reviewed, and the claim of an informed US plan has not been independently corroborated by US officials in what this desk reviewed. This is a fast-moving claim; treat the specifics as unconfirmed pending an on-record US or Iranian government statement.

## Fake Resistance: Israel's response to the NAZA documentary escalates further

The institutional response to the Venice-feted documentary "NAZA" — which alleges an AI-assisted IDF targeting process in Gaza that knowingly accepted a high projected civilian toll — has sharpened again. IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has ordered a formal legal review of the film's claims, reportedly describing them internally as "blood libels"; Netanyahu has said he will advance legislation to revoke the citizenship of "anyone who slanders IDF soldiers"; Culture Minister Miki Zohar has accused the filmmakers of treason; and the government has called for a Shin Bet investigation into both the directors and the serving or former soldiers who gave testimony in the film. The film's central quantified claim — a strike said to have been authorized with an anticipated toll of up to 500 civilian deaths — remains, on the public record reviewed, untied to any identifiable target, date, location, commanding officer or confirmed casualty count. Full evidentiary rundown is on the Fake Resistance desk.

## Watch next

Whether Israeli, Palestinian Authority or Hamas officials issue further statements on today's West Bank attack and its investigation; confirmation or denial from US officials of the reported Iranian claim about renewed strikes; the scope and findings of the IDF's formal legal review of the NAZA allegations; and any Shin Bet action regarding the film's soldier-witnesses.

publication.title: Father of six killed in West Bank shooting attack on Yom Kippur eve; Netanyahu vows to "hold them all accountable"
publication.summary: Netanel Shukrun, 36, was shot dead at the Ein Raya spring in the central West Bank while visiting with his son. The IDF's Duvdevan unit arrested the gunman hours later, and Prime Minister Netanyahu ordered security reinforcements to the West Bank while vowing accountability "in Gaza, in Lebanon, and in Judea and Samaria."
publication.body:
A gunman opened fire on Israelis bathing at the Ein Raya spring in the central West Bank on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, killing Netanel Shukrun, 36, a father of six from the settlement of Alei Zahav, according to the Jerusalem Post and Haaretz. Shukrun was reported to have been visiting the spring with his son at the time of the attack.

Initial reports described the assailant firing from a red Mitsubishi SUV bearing Palestinian Authority license plates before exiting the vehicle, continuing the attack on foot, and fleeing the scene. The IDF said soldiers from its Duvdevan undercover counterterrorism unit, acting on intelligence from the Shin Bet security service and Israel Police, located and arrested the suspect approximately three hours later at a nearby hospital. The military did not, in the sources reviewed, disclose the suspect's identity, motive statement, or any organizational affiliation at the time of writing.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded by saying "no terrorist is immune, nor are those who assisted them," and that Israel "will hold them all accountable — in Gaza, in Lebanon, and in Judea and Samaria." He instructed Israeli security forces to send reinforcements into the West Bank and to impose closures and carry out arrests. Separately, and in what wire reporting described as part of the broader West Bank security posture rather than a direct response to this specific attack, the IDF detained 35 Palestinians in the West Bank village of al-Mughayyir and seized 15 vehicles.

The attack came as the IDF also reported killing three Hamas operatives, including two identified as October 7, 2023 participants, in strikes in Gaza over the weekend — the backdrop against which Netanyahu's multi-front "accountable" statement was made. No Palestinian Authority or Hamas statement responding specifically to the Ein Raya spring attack was available in the sources reviewed. This article will be updated as investigators release further detail on the suspect and any legal proceedings.

publication.title: Reported claim: NAZA documentary alleges IDF used AI-assisted targeting that knowingly accepted mass civilian casualties in Gaza
publication.summary: The Venice-awarded documentary NAZA, built on interviews with 24 current and former Israeli military intelligence personnel, alleges the IDF used an AI-assisted targeting process in Gaza that knowingly accepted high projected civilian death tolls. Israel's institutional response has escalated: a formal IDF legal review, a proposed citizenship-revocation law, a treason accusation against the directors, and a call for a Shin Bet investigation of the filmmakers and their soldier sources.
publication.body:
NAZA, a documentary by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor built on interviews with 24 current and former Israeli military intelligence personnel, alleges that the IDF used an AI-assisted targeting system in Gaza that identified strike targets while knowingly and systematically accepting high projected civilian casualty tolls. Its most quantified claim, as reported by outlets including ABC News, NBC News and France 24, describes a strike the filmmakers say was authorized with an anticipated toll of up to 500 civilian deaths. The film won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice International Film Festival and was reported to have received a lengthy standing ovation at its premiere.

The IDF has denied the film's central allegations, calling them a distortion of how targeting decisions are made and specifically rejecting the 500-casualty claim as "completely false." That denial has since been followed by a marked escalation in Israel's institutional response. IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has ordered a formal legal review of the film's claims, describing them internally, according to reporting reviewed for this update, as "blood libels." Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he will advance legislation to revoke the citizenship of "anyone who slanders IDF soldiers." Culture Minister Miki Zohar has accused the directors of treason and called for their citizenship to be revoked. And the government has called for a Shin Bet investigation into both the filmmakers and the serving or former soldiers who gave testimony in the film.

What remains true of the underlying claim has not changed since this record was first published: the film's central quantified allegation — a strike said to have been authorized with an anticipated toll of up to 500 civilian deaths — has not, on the public record reviewed for this update, been tied by the filmmakers or by reporting on the film to an identifiable target, date, location, commanding officer or confirmed casualty count. The soldiers quoted in the film are reported to have spoken anonymously, which supports the credibility of firsthand testimony while limiting independent verification of specifics.

What is new is that Israel's response now extends well beyond disputing the claim on the merits. A citizenship-revocation law aimed at critics of the military, a treason accusation against journalists, and a state security investigation reaching the soldiers who provided the film's underlying testimony are significant developments in their own right, independent of whether the film's central allegation is ultimately verified or refuted. Readers should weigh both halves of this story: an allegation against the IDF that remains short on independently verifiable specifics, and a state response to that allegation that itself raises questions about legal process and press freedom that deserve separate scrutiny.
